title: THE MAN WHO ENTERED PARADISE WITHOUT EVER BEING BAPTIZED
paragraphs: THE MAN WHO ENTERED PARADISE WITHOUT EVER BEING BAPTIZED

If water baptism is necessary for salvation, how did a dying criminal receive a promise of paradise from Jesus Himself? Three Scriptures. One uncomfortable question. And a truth about grace that could change how you understand salvation forever.
He had no time to change his life.
No opportunity to repair what he had destroyed. No chance to repay the people he had hurt. No years of good behavior to prove that his repentance was genuine.
And certainly no opportunity to climb down from his cross, find a river, and be baptized.
He was dying.
His hands were restrained. His body was broken. His past was catching up with him, and his future appeared to be measured in minutes.
But hanging beside him was Jesus Christ.
And what happened between those two dying men raises one of the most important questions a Christian can ever ask.
Does water baptism save us, or does baptism testify to the salvation we receive through Jesus Christ?
Because if we get this wrong, we risk making one of two devastating mistakes.
We might tell a genuinely repentant sinner that Christ cannot save him until a religious ceremony has been performed.
Or we might tell someone who claims to follow Jesus that His command to be baptized is optional and unimportant.
Neither mistake should be taken lightly.
The answer matters to the person who has believed in Jesus but has never been baptized.
It matters to the mother praying over her dying child.
It matters to the prisoner who encounters the Gospel behind bars.
It matters to the elderly man who finally surrenders to Christ in a hospital bed.
And it matters to the person who was baptized years ago but has never truly repented.
Perhaps that person is reading this right now.
Before we go any further, hold on to one question.
If baptism is what makes a sinner acceptable to God, what exactly happened on that cross when Jesus promised paradise to a man who had nothing left to offer Him?
The answer begins with a conversation almost swallowed by the noise of Calvary.
Luke tells us that two criminals were crucified alongside Jesus. One joined in mocking Him. The other recognized something extraordinary.
He understood that he deserved condemnation for his crimes. He recognized that Jesus had done nothing wrong.
Then he turned toward the Savior and made a request.
“Jesus, remember me when thou comest in thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, ASV)
That was it.
No elaborate prayer.
No public testimony before a congregation.
No baptismal pool.
Just a guilty man acknowledging the innocence and kingship of Jesus, placing his final hope in the One dying beside him.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To-day shalt thou be with me in Paradise.” (Luke 23:43, ASV)
Read that again.
Jesus did not tell him to wait until someone could perform a ceremony.
He did not say that forgiveness was available only after the man completed a religious requirement.
He promised him paradise.
The Greek text records the heart of that promise:
Σήμερον μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ.
Sēmeron met’ emou esē en tō paradeisō.
“Today you will be with me in Paradise.”
The words μετ’ ἐμοῦ — met’ emou — “with me” are especially beautiful.
The criminal's hope was not merely that he would escape punishment.
His hope was that he would be with Jesus.
And Jesus personally assured him of it.

We should be careful here. Luke does not provide a complete biography of this criminal, so we cannot prove that he had never received any kind of earlier baptism. What the account does establish is that Jesus promised him paradise without requiring a baptism to be performed after his confession.
That is a significant fact.

Some Christians point out that this event occurred before Jesus' resurrection and before the missionary command of Matthew 28:19. That observation deserves consideration. It means we should not build an entire doctrine of Christian baptism on this episode alone.
But we must not dismiss what the episode reveals about Jesus.
The Savior has authority to forgive sinners, and the dying man's hope rested entirely on Him.
Not on his ability to complete a ceremony.
Not on his opportunity to demonstrate years of obedience.
On Jesus.
And that brings us to a passage that appears, at first glance, to complicate everything.
Acts 2:38.
Peter had just preached to a crowd in Jerusalem.
He proclaimed that the Jesus they had crucified was both Lord and Christ.
The people were pierced to the heart.
They asked, “Brethren, what shall we do?” (Acts 2:37, ASV)
Peter responded:
“Repent ye, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ unto the remission of your sins; and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.” (Acts 2:38, ASV)
There it is.
Repent.
Be baptized.
For the forgiveness of sins.
How can we read those words and pretend baptism is unimportant?
We cannot.
Peter did not treat baptism as a meaningless religious decoration.
He proclaimed repentance and baptism as the appropriate response to the crucified and risen Christ.
In the Greek text, the phrase is:
μετανοήσατε καὶ βαπτισθήτω ἕκαστος ὑμῶν
Metanoēsate kai baptisthētō hekastos hymōn.
“Repent, and let each one of you be baptized.”
The word μετανοήσατε — metanoēsate is a command to repent. Biblical repentance involves a genuine turning toward God, not merely feeling embarrassed about the consequences of sin.
The word βαπτισθήτω — baptisthētō commands that each person be baptized.
Peter's message was not, “Believe whatever you want, continue living however you please, and call yourself saved.”
His message demanded a response.
But there is another Greek expression in the verse that Christians have debated for centuries:
εἰς ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν
Eis aphesin tōn hamartiōn.
“For the forgiveness of sins.”

The preposition eis can express direction, purpose, or result depending on context. Some interpreters argue that baptism is commanded because forgiveness has already been received. Others understand Peter to connect repentance and baptism with receiving forgiveness.
We should not pretend that the Greek grammar automatically settles this disagreement.
It does not.
Faithful Christians from different theological traditions have understood the relationship between baptism and forgiveness differently.
The question, then, is not whether Acts 2:38 matters.
It absolutely matters.
The question is how to understand it alongside everything else Scripture teaches about salvation.
And this is where the story becomes even more revealing.
In Acts 10, Peter preached the Gospel in the house of Cornelius.
He announced that everyone who believes in Jesus receives forgiveness of sins through His name.
Then something extraordinary happened.
Before Peter finished speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon those who were listening.
They had not yet been baptized in water.
Yet God had already given them the Holy Spirit.
Peter recognized what had happened and asked:
“Can any man forbid the water, that these should not be baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit as well as we?” (Acts 10:47, ASV)
Think about the order.
They heard the Gospel.
They believed.
They received the Holy Spirit.
Then Peter commanded them to be baptized.
Water baptism followed God's evident work among them.
And Peter did not conclude that baptism was therefore unnecessary.
He commanded it.
This account offers powerful evidence that water baptism is not an absolute prerequisite for God to give His Spirit to believers.
At the same time, it shows that receiving God's grace is not a reason to refuse Christ's command.
Grace did not make baptism meaningless. Grace gave them every reason to obey.
And that distinction matters.
Imagine a man standing outside a church.
For years, he has carried guilt that nobody knows about.
He has lied to his wife.
He has disappointed his children.
He has built a respectable public image while privately becoming someone he barely recognizes.
One Sunday, he hears the Gospel.
Not a motivational speech.
Not a promise that life will suddenly become easy.
He hears that Jesus Christ died for sinners, was buried, and rose again.
He hears that forgiveness is offered through the Savior he has spent his life ignoring.
And something breaks inside him.
For the first time in years, he stops defending himself.
He confesses his sin.
He turns to Christ in faith.
He asks for mercy.
Now imagine that, before his scheduled baptism, he dies unexpectedly.
Would we say that Jesus was willing to forgive him but could not receive him because he had not yet entered the water?
That is not the conclusion I believe the whole testimony of Scripture requires.
Paul writes:
The Greek says:
Τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως.
Tē gar chariti este sesōsmenoi dia pisteōs.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith.”
The expression σεσῳσμένοι — sesōsmenoi describes the state of having been saved.
And Paul identifies grace as the source and faith as the means through which salvation is received.
Our confidence rests in God's gift, not our personal achievement.
But someone may ask a very reasonable question.
Doesn't Peter explicitly say that baptism saves us?
Yes.
And we must face that passage rather than avoid it.
First Peter 3:21 declares:

“Which also after a true likeness doth now save you, even baptism, not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the interrogation of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.” (ASV)
That is a difficult verse for anyone who casually says baptism has nothing to do with salvation.
Peter actually uses the words “baptism ... doth now save you.”
The Greek begins:
ὃ καὶ ὑμᾶς ἀντίτυπον νῦν σῴζει βάπτισμα
Ho kai hymas antitypon nyn sōzei baptisma.
Corresponding to the earlier image, baptism now saves you.
But Peter immediately qualifies what he means.
οὐ σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου
Ou sarkos apothesis rhypou.
“Not the removal of dirt from the flesh.”
Peter explicitly refuses to reduce baptism's saving significance to an external washing.

He continues with a phrase involving the Greek word ἐπερώτημα — eperōtēma, whose precise sense is debated. It has been understood as an appeal, request, or pledge relating to a good conscience toward God.
The verse then identifies the decisive foundation:
δι’ ἀναστάσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
Di’ anastaseōs Iēsou Christou.
“Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.”
Notice where Peter directs our attention.
Not to the magical power of water.
Not to the personal holiness of the minister.
Not to the physical act considered apart from Christ.
To the resurrection of Jesus.

Christians who understand baptism sacramentally rightly emphasize that Peter speaks of baptism as more than an empty symbol. They see it as a means through which God graciously acts, never as a human accomplishment that earns salvation.

Christians who understand baptism primarily as the outward sign of saving faith emphasize Peter's qualification that salvation is not accomplished by the mere washing of the body. They understand baptism's saving language in relation to the faith and appeal to God that baptism expresses.
Both readings must take Peter's words seriously.
And both must recognize this:
No water possesses saving power independent of the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
That is the center of the passage.
It is also the center of the Gospel.
Consider what Paul says in Romans 6.
He describes believers as having been baptized into Christ Jesus and into His death, buried with Him through baptism, and raised to walk in newness of life.
What an extraordinary picture.
Going down into the water.
Burial.
Coming up from the water.
Resurrection.
The old life no longer holds the final claim.
Jesus Christ has conquered death.
But Romans 6 is not merely about performing a ceremony. It is about belonging to Christ and living in the reality of His death and resurrection.
And this is where the discussion must become personal.
Because there is another danger.
A danger that may be even more common than theological confusion.
It is possible to be baptized in water while continuing to resist the Lord Jesus Christ.
A person can remember the exact date of a baptism.
Remember the pastor who performed it.
Remember the church.
Remember the photographs.
Remember the celebration afterward.
And still live without repentance, trust, or love for Jesus.
Water baptism must never be used as a substitute for the living Savior.
The New Testament repeatedly calls people to believe in Christ.
In Acts 16, a terrified jailer asked Paul and Silas:
“Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
They answered:
“Believe on the Lord Jesus, and thou shalt be saved, thou and thy house.” (Acts 16:30–31, ASV)
Later in the same account, the jailer and his household were baptized.
Once again, faith and baptism belong closely together.
They are not enemies.
They are not competing paths to God.
The Gospel creates faith, and faith is called to express itself in obedience.
This is why the question should never become an excuse for disobedience.
If you have trusted Jesus Christ and have the opportunity to be baptized, why would you deliberately refuse a command given by the One you call Lord?
Jesus instructed His disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19).
Baptism is not an optional invention of church culture.
It is part of Christ's commission.
The Ethiopian official in Acts 8 responded to the message of Jesus by asking to be baptized when he saw water.
The believers in Acts 2 were baptized.
The household of Cornelius was baptized.
The Philippian jailer and his household were baptized.
Again and again, baptism appears as the natural response of people receiving the Gospel.
Not because Christians should place their confidence in a ritual instead of Jesus.
But because following Jesus means taking His words seriously.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to stop arguing and start examining our hearts.
Have you been postponing baptism because you are afraid of what people will think?
Are you embarrassed to identify publicly with Jesus?
Have you told yourself that faith is private, even while Christ calls His disciples to acknowledge Him openly?
Or are you trusting in a baptism from childhood while resisting the very Savior whose name was spoken over you?
These are not questions designed to shame you.
They are questions worth bringing honestly before God.
Because Jesus did not die merely to make us more religious.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
And His resurrection announces that sin and death do not have the final word.
The thief on the cross had no future in which to demonstrate a long life of discipleship.
But he had Jesus.
The crowd in Acts 2 had an opportunity to repent and be baptized.
And Peter commanded them to respond.
Cornelius and his household received the Holy Spirit before water baptism.
And Peter commanded their baptism too.
First Peter 3:21 speaks powerfully about baptism's saving significance while directing us beyond bodily washing to a good conscience toward God through Christ's resurrection.
Taken together, these passages resist simplistic slogans.
They call us to hold grace, faith, repentance, baptism, and obedience in their proper relationship to Jesus Christ.

My conclusion, from reading these passages together, is that water baptism is commanded for disciples of Jesus, but the physical act itself is not an absolute condition that limits Christ's power to save a genuinely repentant believer who cannot receive it.

This is the position commonly expressed in many evangelical Protestant traditions. Other Christian traditions understand baptism as an ordinary means by which God grants saving grace, while also recognizing that God's mercy is not necessarily limited to the visible administration of the sacrament.
The disagreement is real, and it should not be hidden.
But we should be equally clear about what Christians can affirm together.
Jesus saves.
His death and resurrection are essential.
Repentance and faith matter.
Baptism matters.
And no human being has the authority to replace Christ with a religious performance.
The water does not deserve our worship.
Jesus does.
The ceremony is not our Redeemer.
Jesus is.
The minister is not the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
Jesus is.
And when baptism is rightly understood, it directs our attention toward Him.
Now return with me to Calvary.
Picture the dying criminal one final time.
His breathing is failing.
His strength is disappearing.
The world has already passed judgment on him.
He cannot make himself respectable.
He cannot erase the damage he has done.
He cannot purchase another opportunity.
And he cannot save himself.
Yet beside him hangs the sinless Son of God.
The One who will rise from the dead.
The One whose blood is sufficient to cleanse sinners.
The One who has authority to forgive.
And the criminal asks to be remembered.
Not because he has become worthy.
But because he has recognized the King.
Jesus does not answer with a list of achievements the man must complete.
He gives him a promise.
Paradise.
With Him.
That is the beauty of grace.
But do not misunderstand grace.
Grace is not permission to remain in rebellion against God.
Grace is not a license to ignore the commands of Jesus.
Grace is not a religious loophole that allows us to claim Christ while refusing to follow Him.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace transforms.
Grace teaches us to obey.
And that is why the person who has genuinely trusted Christ should not treat baptism with indifference.
If you have never been baptized as a believer and are convicted that you should be, speak with a faithful local church about taking that step.
Not to purchase God's love.
Not to impress other Christians.
Not to prove that you are better than anyone else.
But to identify openly with the Lord who died and rose again.
And if you have already been baptized, do not stop at the memory of the water.
Ask yourself whether your life is bearing the fruit of repentance and faith.
Do you love Jesus?
Are you learning to obey Him?
When you fall, do you return to Him in repentance?
Are you becoming more honest about your sin and more dependent on His mercy?
Because the Christian life is not sustained by looking back to one ceremony while neglecting the Savior every day afterward.
We need Christ today.
We will need Him tomorrow.
And we will need Him when our final hour comes.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes because someone you loved died before being baptized.
I cannot pronounce with certainty the eternal destiny of a particular person whose heart I did not know.
That judgment belongs to God.
But I can tell you this.
The Lord Jesus is not powerless when circumstances prevent a dying sinner from entering baptismal water.
And the thief on the cross is a profound reminder that no desperate sinner should be told that the door of Christ's mercy has closed merely because time has run out for a ceremony.
Perhaps you are reading this because you have spent years running from God.
You know the language of Christianity.
You know how to look spiritual.
You know how to smile when someone asks how your faith is doing.
But inside, something is terribly wrong.
You are exhausted from pretending.
You are afraid that if people knew your secret struggles, they would never look at you the same way again.
Hear the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come to congratulate the righteous.
He came to call sinners to repentance.
He did not shed His blood for people who could save themselves.
He came to seek and save the lost.
Your sin is serious.
Your need for repentance is real.
But the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than your ability to repair yourself.
Turn to Him.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Follow Him.
And do not allow a theological debate to distract you from the Savior standing at the center of it.
Because one day, the question will no longer be whether you won an argument about baptism.
The question will be whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
And there is something else I want you to remember.
The criminal on the cross could not climb down to demonstrate his devotion.
But you and I, while God gives us breath and opportunity, can respond to His Word.
We can repent.
We can believe.
We can be baptized.
We can forgive those who have hurt us.
We can make peace where we have caused division.
We can confess what we have hidden.
We can begin walking in obedience today.
Not to earn the cross.
Because of the cross.
Salvation is not a trophy for the religiously accomplished. It is the gift of God, received through faith in Jesus Christ, whose grace produces a life of obedience.
And when the water is understood in the light of the cross, baptism becomes a beautiful proclamation of the Savior to whom we belong.
This is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From spiritual death to new life.
Not because we managed to rewrite our own stories.
But because Jesus Christ entered our brokenness, bore our sin, conquered the grave, and opened the way to the Father.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not to win a debate.
Not to start another argument between denominations.
But because there may be someone reading these words who has been carrying this question for years.
Do you believe baptism is necessary to receive salvation, or do you understand it as an act of obedience that follows saving faith?
And more importantly, what Scripture has shaped your conviction?
If you have been hiding behind religion while avoiding genuine repentance, perhaps your honest response is “Jesus, change my heart.”
There is no need to pretend here.
We are sinners who need a Savior.
And we are learning to walk in His grace.

If someone came to your mind while reading this, consider tagging them—not to embarrass them or pressure them, but to invite them into a conversation that may help them understand the Gospel more clearly.

Somewhere among your friends may be a believer who has never understood baptism, a family member who has confused religion with salvation, or someone quietly wondering whether Jesus could still forgive them.
Your simple act of sharing could put Scripture in front of a person who might never have searched for it.
But I also want to speak to those who believe this kind of ministry is worth sustaining.
Producing and sharing biblical teaching, making discipleship resources available, and reaching people who may never walk into a church building all require ongoing effort and support.
Our desire is to keep making biblical nourishment accessible while continuing to expand the work.
It is a practical way of helping this ministry continue producing, distributing, and expanding resources centered on Christ.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing and cheerful, not reluctant or forced (2 Corinthians 9:7).
These products are not the heart of our mission.
Jesus Christ is.
The resources, the articles, the books, and the community exist to serve that greater purpose.
Read the Scriptures.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage another believer.
Speak to a struggling friend about Jesus.
Faithful service to God is not measured by the size of a monthly payment.
Every gift should be freely offered, and every act of obedience should be directed toward the glory of Christ.
Because in the end, our mission is not to build a kingdom around a Facebook page.
It is to point people toward the Kingdom of God.
Toward repentance.
Toward forgiveness.
Toward the cross.
Toward the empty tomb.
Toward the Savior who can receive a dying criminal and transform a living sinner.
And when everything else fades—our religious arguments, our accomplishments, our reputations, even the memories of our most important moments—only one foundation will be sufficient.
Jesus Christ.
So here is the question I want to leave with you.
When your own final hour comes, what will you be trusting?
The religious things you have done?
The approval of other people?
The belief that you were somehow good enough?
Or the crucified and risen Son of God?
Be baptized in obedience to Christ.
Take His commands seriously.
Walk in repentance.
But never confuse the sign of belonging to Jesus with the Savior Himself.
The dying thief had no time left to build a religious record—but he was not beyond the reach of the King who was dying beside him.
